content:
The Leader introduced the report.
 
I am pleased to
present the Quarter 3 Corporate Performance Report to Cabinet.
This report is
vital in helping us understand how our in-year activity is
delivering against our Corporate and Improvement Plan, and
crucially how we are meeting the expectations we have set for
ourselves as a Labour administration.
Because for us,
performance is not just about numbers. It is about delivering on
Labour’s priorities: strong, accountable local government,
high-quality public services, and real outcomes for our residents
particularly those who rely on us most.
Despite the
backdrop of upcoming elections, it is important that we recognise
both how far we have come and how far we still have to go to become a fully sustainable authority.
Since the intervention, we have made significant progress, and this
report reflects a council that is more open, more transparent, and
more honest about its performance.
We do not shy away
from our challenges. Instead, we are building a culture that
reflects Labour values one that celebrates success but also
confronts underperformance head-on. We are clear where things are
working, and equally clear where improvement is needed.
This
quarter’s report shows good progress against the commitments
we set for this year. It also highlights the sheer breadth of work
being delivered across the council. I want to take this opportunity
to thank our officers, who are not only maintaining services but
actively improving them for our communities.
Importantly, we are
stretching ourselves against a wide range of performance measures.
Where performance is not where it should be, we are identifying
issues early and taking action. Areas
such as smoking rates amongst residents and the culture of
recycling demonstrates the complexity of the challenges we face but
also our determination to take innovative approaches and drive
improvement.
Our approach to
performance management is also maturing. We are increasingly
bringing together teams across different disciplines to tackle
deep-rooted and complex issues ensuring that we don’t just
monitor performance but actively intervene to improve outcomes.
This reflects our commitment to joined-up, efficient public
services that work for residents.
I am also
encouraged by the work underway to better align assurance functions
such as Risk, Audit, Finance and People Services. By sharing data
and insight more effectively, we are building a more intelligent
picture of how the council is performing strengthening
accountability and decision-making.
Over the past year,
these reports have given Cabinet the assurance that our Corporate
Plan priorities are being delivered and that our improvement
journey is on track. It is also reassuring that the
Commissioners’ sixth report reflects both the progress we
have made and the areas where further work is needed demonstrating
a shared and honest assessment of our position.
There has been a clear step change in how
we hold ourselves to account. We have strengthened the quality and
reliability of our data, aligned it with recognised standards, and
ensured it is comparable with similar councils. Meaning we are more
transparent, more credible, and more accountable to our
residents.
With these stronger
foundations now in place, we must continue to build on this
progress. There is no room for complacency. As we move into the
next year and towards our final year as Thurrock Council we must
ensure we remain focused, disciplined, and ambitious in delivering
for our communities.
 
Councillor L Watson commented that she was
pleased to see the Individual Health Assessments for Childrens Services on there and noted the
improvement and good work being completed by the Corporate
Parenting committee and Children’s Overview and Scrutiny
Committee.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1Cabinet noted the
quarterly corporate performance report at Appendix 1 and progress
made up to the end of the second quarter of 2025/26 in delivering
the corporate and improvement plan.
 
2.2Cabinet considered
recommending any areas of concern within the remits of the Overview
and Scrutiny Committees to the chairs of those respective
committees.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to review the Quarter 3 Corporate Performance Report, highlighting progress and areas for improvement in delivering the corporate and improvement plan.

content:
Councillor J Kent introduced the report.
 
Councillor Rigby was permitted to ask her
question.
 
I can see the
advantages of a joint strategy. However given the significant
industrialisation, the proposed Lower Thames Crossing and high
health inequality levels in Thurrock, what measures will be put in
place to ensure the action plan will adequately and fairly address
issues in the borough?
 
Councillor J Kent explained that the joint
strategy helps to work in partnership as air quality is a trans
boundary issue with 50% of air pollution coming from outside the
borough. The strategy recognises the differing needs of each
authority and allows for flexibility to take both individual and
collaborative needs into account. Officers regularly meet with
officers across Essex in a working group regarding the
strategy.
 
Councillor Rigby asked the following
supplementary question.
 
In the report
indoor pollution is mentioned, what are the plans to tackle that
aspect.
 
Councillor J Kent responded that this will be
the same as outdoor pollution and will be reported on at the
correct time.
 
The Leader queried if this is separate from
the dust issue in Tilbury.
 
Councillor J Kent responded that it is
separate and Councillor Hooper has spent
a great deal of time on this issue and is setting up a reporting
line to help collate in real time and gather a body of evidence to
confirm where the dust is coming from.
 
Councillor Hooper responded that a public
helpline will be in place in late spring / Summer which is when the
dust is an issue. When it is wet the dust stays on the ground and
is less of an issue. The council is trying to work with the Port of
Tilbury to reduce emissions or to be held to account if they are
not meeting their obligations. A report is going to Place Overview
and Scrutiny next week. The council wants the Port to be good
neighbours. The money is there and it is
for officers to put in the work and start the helpline.
 
The Leader responded that she notices when the
dust is bad in the summer as she has to
clean it off her garden furniture daily at its worst.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1 Cabinet agreed to formally adopt the Strategy as
local policy, as originally approved at Cabinet in November
2024.
 
Reason for the
decision: as outlined in the report
This decision is
subject to call-in
topline: The Council has decided to formally adopt a joint strategy to address air quality issues in Thurrock.

content:
The Leader introduced the report.
 
Thames Freeport
represents one of the most significant economic opportunities in
our regions recent history. Spanning an economic zone across
Thurrock and the London Boroughs of Havering and Barking &
Dagenham, the Freeport is projected to create 21,000 jobs and
attract 4.6 billion of investment over the next 25 years
transforming communities and driving long-term growth across east
London and south Essex.
This Council plays
a central and responsible role in making that vision a reality. We
act as Accountable Body, ensuring proper assurance and oversight of
public funds; as a delivery partner, actively working to realise
the Freeport objectives; and as billing authority, administering
the business rates reliefs that underpin the programmes financial
model. These roles carry real obligations, and this Cabinet report
sets out how we intend to fulfil them for the year ahead.
The Freeport is now
moving from start-up into a genuine delivery phase, with investment
beginning to flow and projects taking shape on the ground. This
paper asks Cabinet to approve 10.95 million to fund the 2026/27
Freeport Business Plan, drawing on Government funding provided
through Section 31 grant payments within the agreed Memorandum of
Understanding. It also seeks delegated authority for officers, in
consultation with Members, to approve the final business plan and
sign the annual Grant Funding Agreement once the necessary
assurance checks and subsidy control assessments have been
completed.
I am pleased to
bring this report to Cabinet. The decisions we take today will
ensure that the Council continues to meet its responsibilities,
that Thames Freeport Limited can press ahead with delivery, and
that our residents and businesses can begin to benefit from the
jobs, investment and regeneration this programme will bring.
 
There were no comments or questions from
members.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1Cabinet approved a funding
allocation of £10.95m for Thames Freeport for 2026/27, in
line with the submitted Business Plan, noting that this sits within
the maximum funding envelope determined by the NNDR1 return.
Delegate authority to the s151 Officer, in consultation with the
Assistant Chief Executive and the Leader, to agree any in?year
adjustments to this allocation within the confirmed funding
envelope.
 
2.2 Cabinet delegated authority to the Assistant Chief
Executive in consultation with Section 151 Officer and the Leader,
to approve the Thames Freeport Business and Finance Plan for
2026/27 following completion of Accountable Body due diligence,
governance checks and subsidy control assessment.
 
2.3Cabinet delegated authority to
the Section 151 Officer, in consultation with the Assistant Chief
Executive and the Leader to approve and release funding for
individual projects within the 2026/27 Business and Finance Plan
with a value of £250,000 or above, subject to:
·      
submission of a full business case
·      
completion of a Green Book compliant appraisal
·      
confirmation of affordability within the S31 grant relating to
retained business rates.
 

2.4  Cabinet delegated authority to the Assistant Chief Executive in
consultation with Section 151 Officer and the Leader to enter into,
vary and sign the Grant Funding Agreement with Thames Freeport
Limited for 2026/27, enabling the release of funds in accordance
with the approved Business and Finance Plan.
Reason for the
decision: as outlined in the report
This decision is
subject to call-in
topline: The Council has decided to approve funding for the Thames Freeport project to support job creation and economic growth in the region.

content:
Councillor L Watson introduced the report, she
explained that it is an ambitious project to build around 2800
homes, centred around a new town centre, a new bridge over the
railway and a new primary school.
 
Councillor L Watson confirmed there are some
changes to the previous scheme proposed. Councillor L Watson
thanked the Purfleet forum for everything they have done and noted
that residents have waited decades for this.
 
Councillor J Kent commented that there has
been a history of over promising and under delivering on Purfleet
and queried what will be different this time.
 
Councillor L Watson responded that the old
scheme included private funding, this one is fully backed by Homes
England. They want to build these homes and see it as a real
opportunity in Purfleet.
 
Councillor Hooper queried if the homes will be
affordable for Thurrock people, available for rent and Thurrock
residents given priority to them.
 
Councillor L Watson responded that there will
be a mixed form of tenure including shared ownership and rented
properties.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1Cabinet noted that Muse
Places are the preferred partner for delivery of the regeneration
of Purfleet-on-Thames;
2.2Cabinet agreed that
officers begin negotiations on the terms of a development agreement
with Muse Places and undertake due diligence on the
issues still to be resolved as set out in this report (to include,
but not limited to funding, planning and legal
considerations) with the Council and Muse Places working at
their own cost and risk during this process;
2.3Cabinet noted that any
proposed Development Agreement will be brought back to a future
cabinet meeting for decision.
2.4Cabinet noted that the
Council is allocating £450k from its Freeport Counterfactual
Reserve to fund Council only costs incurred to deliver
recommendation 2.2 above, including sourcing external specialist
support and advice
topline: The Council has decided to approve recommendations for the regeneration of Purfleet-on-Thames, with Muse Places as the preferred partner for the project.

content:
Councillor Hartstean introduced the
report.
 
Non-Executive Member Councillor Rigby was
invited to ask her question.
 
The recent Adults and Health informal meeting
with parents of autistic and neurodiverse children and adults with
lived experience, highlighted that although they have been engaged
with they felt they had not been listened to. This procurement is
for young people with high needs autism but from this, how will you
measure from your reviews to date and from formal assessment ahead,
that the feedback from young people, families and carers will be
truly integrated into future provision guidelines?
 
Councillor Hartstean responded that she was
also present at the meeting and heard the concerns from parents and
young people. A Council wide review is taking place for children
and adults with autism and neurodiversity, this commissioning
exercise is part of that. A group of parents have provided feedback
on this service and parents will score one part of the tender
commission.
 
Councillor Rigby asked a supplemental
question. This is a cost saving exercise but there is also an
ongoing increase in demand, can you give reassurance that the
correct care will be given even if it turns out to be more
expensive.
 
Councillor Hartstean responded that referrals
will be done through a panel. There will be a bespoke package for
each young person. Previously, it has been a 24 month package but
some young people may only need 12 months so this will be a cost
saving.
 
The Leader queried if there are more children
with autism and neurodiversity or are we better at diagnosing.
 
Councillor Hartstean responded that it is
probably a combination of both. Premature children have much better
chances of survival, parents are much more aware of symptoms and
diagnosing has become better. There is a statutory duty to meet
needs regardless of a diagnosis.
 
RESOLVED:

up to two years, for an Autism Support Programme for Young People
Aged 18-25, commencing on 1st September 2026.

following: Executive Director - Adults and Health and Executive
Director - Childrens Services in consultation with the Section 151
Officer, Cabinet Member for Childrens Services, Education and
Community Safety and Cabinet Member for Health and Well-being and
Social Housing

content:
Councillor Hooper introduced the report and
explained that in May 2025 a Care Quality Commission (CQC)
inspection took place. Thurrock Council Adult services received s
high/ good rating.
 
An Improvement plan has been put together
resulting from the inspection and this will go to the Adults and
Health Overview and Scrutiny meeting in February hopefully and then
on to Cabinet in March.
 
Non-Executive Member Councillor Rigby was
permitted to ask her question.
 

The Commissioners comments describe the importance of the
improvement plan aligning with the Council's wider transformation
plan. How will you ensure this is achieved?

 
Councillor Hooper responded that as stated
earlier the improvement plan will go to Overview and Scrutiny
before Cabinet and the improvement plan will also be included in
the Corporate Plan and the Transformation Roadmap.
 
Councillor Rigby asked the following
supplemental question:
 

Will you be working with all sectors to ensure it all fits in?

 
Councillor Hooper agreed that he would and
confirmed that he works closely with Councillor Watson. It was also
brought up at the Health and Wellbeing Board yesterday, so all
parties and sectors are influencing the plan.
 
Councillor Hartstean thanked everyone involved
from social workers to managers.
 
Councillor Watson queries the area of
development in joint strategic needs assessments and how far behind
the service is on that.
 
Councillor Hooper confirmed that he thinks
they can get this done fairly quickly.
The Directorate were already aware of where they were weak in areas
and work is ongoing to improve these areas.
 
Councillor Heath highlighted that this shows
what can be achieved through dedication and hard work and whilst
the council is in intervention too.
 
The Leader extended her thanks to everyone who
took part in the inspection as being under any inspection is
stressful. The service needs to take on board the learning. The
Leader queried as we go into LGR what steps are being taken to
ensure services of this standard will continue to ensure our next
inspection is just as good.
 
Councillor Hooper stated that Essex and
Southend all got Good ratings but
Thurrock did better. Conversations are starting as to how we can
work together as we move into LGR. We shouldn’t become
tribalist and we should take the positives from Essex and Southend
to help the new council formed. These relationships hold us in a
good place to maintain and improve services as that culture is
already there.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1   Cabinet noted and commented on the positive
findings of the CQC Assessment Report.
 
2.2    Cabinet noted and commented on the
initial areas of development included within the Adult Social Care
CQC Improvement plan to support the ambitions of the Directorate
and ensure continuous improvement.
 
2.3    Cabinet noted that the Adult Social
Care CQC Improvement plan will support the Corporate Roadmap and
Transformation Programme
topline: The Cabinet has decided to discuss the positive findings of a Care Quality Commission inspection and the improvement plan for Adult Social Care services in Thurrock Council.

content:
Councillor Morris-Cook introduced the report
and explained that it provides an update on the council’s
Divestment programme. £661 million pounds has been recovered
which represents 63% of the original portfolio value. A further
£130 million pounds is forecast to be received in the next
year.

Kavannagh is far from being let off the hook and is being pursued.
Professional fees of £5.3 million have been incurred to date
and this is forecast to raise to £10.6 million to 2029. This
is equal to approximately 1% of the amount recovered so far.
 
The Leader stated that understandably it makes
people angry hearing how much money was lost. The Leader queried if
everything has been done to keep up the pressures on the
divestments as the more we get back the
less we have to rely on the Government.
 
Councillor Morris-Cook stated that no stone
will be unturned. There are regular meetings between the S151
officer and Monitoring officer. As we move into LGR there will be
no dilution on this.
 
The Leader responded that she was pleased to
hear that.

divestment programme progress and the impact on the Council’s
CD; (Section 5);

professional advisory fees incurred to date and forecast fees
(Section 6);

continuation of the delegations previously agreed by Cabinet to
enable the implementation of the divestment strategy (Section 4.8);
and
 
2.4Cabinet noted the
decisions taken to deliver the programme to date (Section
6.8).
topline: The council has decided to continue with their Divestment programme, recovering funds and pursuing those responsible for losses.

content:
Councillor V Hartstean introduced the report
and explained that it sought Cabinet’s approval to bring
traded catering services to a close. It is not a statutory duty for
a council to provide this and especially not for a council in
intervention. This will bring Thurrock in line with other Local
Authorities. The schools have been given ample notice to ensure
there is no disruption to the children in Thurrock.
 
Councillor Heath queried if the Portfolio
Holder was confident no child will go hungry at school and queried
who will monitor the standards of the food provided.
 
Councillor Hartstean responded that it is
Schools who have a statutory duty to ensure children eligible for
free school meals are provided for. It is also for schools to
ensure the catering complies with school food standards.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1 Cabinet approved the cessation of the TSCS and the
giving of notice to terminate all current school catering contracts
so that they will come to an end by no later than on
31st July 2026.
 
2.2 Cabinet delegated authority to the Executive
Director of Children’s Services, in consultation with the
Lead Member for Children’s Services, Education and Community
Safety, to take all steps required to terminate the contracts and
work with the schools to facilitate a smooth transition to any
alternate catering service supplier that they identify as their
replacement contractor. 
 
Reason for the
decision: as outlined in the report
This decision is
subject to call-in
topline: The Cabinet has decided to close traded catering services in Thurrock schools

content:
Councillor L Watson introduced the report and
explained that it concerns a National infrastructure project.
National Grid are proposing a 400km transmission line from Norwich
to Tilbury which is critical for national energy resilience. There
will be a visual impact from pylons and a substation. Other
concerns are noise disruption, flood risk, cables sterilising the
ground around them, and heritage risks. The report recommends
submitting a relevant representation highlighting the concerns and
opposing the scheme as currently proposed.
 
The Leader commented that it is important that
Thurrock’s views are heard on this.
 
Councillor Hooper queried if the scheme can be
stopped and what the impact would be locally.
 
Councillor L Watson stated that like the Lower
Thames Crossing the council can submit an opposition but ultimately
as a national project the Secretary of State will make the final
decision. Most developers have got the scheme on their radar.
 
Councillor J Kent stated that he supports the
recommendation and whilst there is a need to get clean energy into
Thurrock he cannot support the scheme as currently proposed as it
does too much damage to Thurrock. Hopefully, with some movements we
can get a scheme we can all agree on.
 
Councillor L Watson confirmed that she will be
proposing an additional recommendation. Cabinet agreed the
additional recommendation outlined at number 3 below.
 
RESOLVED:
(1)
     Cabinet agreed to submit a
Relevant Representation (Appendix A) which identifies the technical
areas that require resolution by National Grid.

(2)      Cabinet opposed the scheme as it
is currently proposed, unless the concerns outlined in Appendix A
are resolved.

(3)      Cabinet
agreed to delegate authority to the Chief Planning Officer in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Good Growth to strengthen
the representation with evidence to support the Council’s
case and examination in public. The core position remains unchanged
and the contents of Appendix A remains the same.

 

Reason for the decision: as outlined in the report

This decision is subject to call-in
topline: The Cabinet has decided to oppose a National infrastructure project for a transmission line due to concerns about its impact on the local area.

content:
At 19.39 Councillor
L Watson left the room.
 
Councillor Morris-Cook introduced the report
and explained that the site is surplus to requirements and part of
the asset disposal programme. The site is 4.5 hectares and does
include informal open space that requires a public notice. Most
concerns received have been about future development and not the
disposal. Any planning application to develop to land will have to
go through the Planning Committee.
 
Councillor V Holloway commented that of all
difficult decisions selling land and assets is the worst. As a
councillor for 14 years it feels wrong to sell green spaces and it
doesn’t feel fair. If the council was my house I know I would
have to sell the contents to keep the house. If the Cabinet says no
then the decision will be taken by commissioners.
 
Councillor Morris-Cook thanked Councillor V
Holloway for her eloquent comments.
 
Councillor Hooper stated that he was also
going to say something that echoed Councillor Holloway’s
comments. Its feels like selling the crown jewels, green spaces are
important places for resident’s wellbeing.  Councillor Hooper queried the advantages to the
people of South Ockendon.
 
Councillor Morris-Cook responded that this
would not be known until it goes to the Planning Committee. There
will be a full consultation and developers will inform the
residents of South Ockendon.
 
Councillor J Kent responded that residents
understand the situation and most objections are about the loss of
green spaces. Cabinet has its hands tied and accept it needs to be
sold. Councillor J Kent stated that he wishes there was some
protection that could be put in place.
 
Councillor Morris-Cook responded that there
are possibilities to have these conversations with the
developers.
 
Councillor J Kent requested if an additional
recommendation could be agreed to that effect.
 
RESOLVED:
 
2.1Following consideration
of the objections received under Section 123 (2A) of the Local
Government Act 1972 and set out in Appendix 4, Cabinet agreed in
principle to the disposal of the Land formerly occupied by the
Culver Centre, South Ockendon (“the Site”) as set out
in Appendix 1
 
2.2Cabinet agreed to delegate authority to
the Executive Director of Place, following consultation with the
Section 151 Officer, Cabinet Member for Finance and
Resources and the Leader to agree the disposal of the Site
including terms and conditions of sale.
 
 
2.3 The Executive Director of Place, S151 Officer, the
Leader and the Portfolio Holder for Resources give further
consideration to the terms of sale having regard to the concerns
expressed by residents in the consultation.
 
Reason for the
decision: as outlined in the report
This decision was
subject to call-in
 
At 19.52 Councillor
L Watson returned to the room.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the disposal of a 4.5 hectare site, including informal open space, in South Ockendon.
